Automated code reviews have become a necessity but they are very difficult to get right.

What do we want from automated code reviews?

- Automated code reviews for straightforward PRs, and escalation to a human when necessary

- Code reviews that improve the code quality by catching issues that humans frequently don’t (and we will see examples of that) but without drowning humans (or other agents) in false positives

- A setup that is fast and cheap, of course

- …and a system that we can adapt to use different models, as the best options considering quality, speed and cost change frequently

We went looking for a setup we could try on our own code. We had two open-source projects, years of pull requests and, conveniently enough, a supply of bugs we had written ourselves.

We found a setup we’re happy to put into production. Our pick is Alibaba Open Code Review (OCR) with Mistral Large 4. At OCR’s lowest effort setting it caught four of the five historical bugs we gave it, and a review usually came back in a few minutes. We added a rule about where to look for tests and a small script that tells CI when a person needs to take a look. We’ve already run it on a live Starlasu pull request .

## Context: Software Factories on the horizon?

Large language models are changing the way we write software, and I have the temptation to go to the whiteboard and imagine the most glorious new way to do software development, building our own flavor of a software factory.

However, scars tell me that the “blank slate” approach just does not work. When processes need to change one needs to do things gradually. You change one piece, you look at what happens, you adapt and only then you move to the next piece. The big bang approach gives you half a day of ego boost but then fails at adoption time, either because you fail to consider some aspects or because humans fail to adapt. Incremental wins the race here.

So where are we with our software development process?

Let’s start by confessing that we are not living in a land of milk and honey as some people claim to be experiencing on LinkedIn. Here in the real world what has already changed for us is that we work with Claude Code or Codex , opening a session and working together with the agent. It works well, and it means that a lot more code gets written in a day than it used to.

Which is good, but that moves the bottleneck somewhere else, and in our case it moved to code review. If the amount of code grows the way it is growing, we cannot keep reviewing all of it by hand, and pretending we can just means that reviews become shallower without anybody saying so. I can type “LGTM” pretty fast now, but it is demeaning, and I die a little bit inside as a professional each time . The alternative of spending all day doing code reviews does not feel tempting either.

So at this stage what needs to be fixed is code reviews.

At Strumenta we have already built our own system for code reviews, which we call Olaf . Before investing more in it we decided to look seriously at what already exists as open-source. This is what we set out to do in this article.

In this article we are going to see:

- A first survey of all open-source reviewers we could find (75) and how we picked one . We will explain the criteria we used to pick it and the ones we used to discard the others.

- How we tested the one we picked , Alibaba Open Code Review (OCR), on two of our open-source projects, using historical bugs and pull requests we believed to be clean.

- Which models we tried and what we learned about configuring them , and, oh boy, we were in for a few surprises.

- How much effort the reviewer should put in , and whether a second model is worth it.

- Quality and price , measured on our runs and projected on six months of activity across all our repositories.

- Why we ended up choosing Mistral , a European provider, over Claude, OpenAI, DeepSeek and the various coding subscriptions.

Let’s get started.

## How Did We Pick the Reviewer?

We started from a list of 75 open-source projects that review pull requests with an LLM. Then we threw away the ones that were just not credible as they were weekend projects with no real adoption. In the end we kept only 20 in the race, worth taking a closer look. Here they are.

Then we applied six filters, one after the other.

- Can we actually use it? We are looking for solutions which are open source for real . For example, Kodus keeps its most interesting parts in enterprise directories you may not modify or host, GitLab Duo needs a subscription in production, and Warden uses a license that is not open source.

- Does it work with more than one model family? We want to be able to switch to different models, so we do not want to tie us to a solution that works only with OpenAI or Anthropic or any other provider, as we are talking about an essential component on how we work.

- Is it agentic? A single-pass reviewer sends the diff to the model once and collects the comments, while an agentic one gives the model tools to read files and search the code, so that it can look at what is around the change. We want the second kind, so we excluded the three tools that are single-pass only: PR-Agent, ChatGPT-CodeReview and genai-code-review.

- Can we use our own key? We want to call the model provider directly, with our own API key, so that the code goes only to the provider we chose. Some tools require instead an intermediary like OpenRouter, as pr-af does, and that is one more company the code passes through. No thank you.

- Does it work on different platforms? Several of these tools work only on GitHub, like Shippie, OpenReview and Pullfrog, while most of our code is on a self-hosted GitLab and the rest on GitHub, so we need a reviewer that supports both.

- Can we run it on our own infrastructure? We want the reviewer to run as a job in our CI, without depending on someone else’s hosting. This excludes OpenReview again, because it runs only on Vercel.

## The selected contenders

Four projects passed all the filters:

The assessments in the table come from reading the code of the four projects.

Of these four we decided to try only one, OCR, and we picked it because of the way it uses the agent, which matters more than it may seem at first. If the agent chooses by itself which files to open, on a large pull request it can end up never opening some of them, while if ordinary code hands every changed file to the model, one call per file, nothing is skipped, but each file is looked at without the code around it. OCR takes a middle road: the changed files are split into groups of related files, ordinary code makes sure that every file ends up in a group and that every group gets reviewed, and the agent working on a group is free to open the rest of the repository whenever it needs context.

The two percentages in the figure come from Kodus, one of the twenty projects on our list, which we excluded because of its license. Kodus lets a team write its own rules for the review, such as “never log personal data”, and at first it checked them with an agent that decided by itself which files to read. When the Kodus developers measured how many violations were actually found, the answer was 40% with GPT-5.4 and 58% with Kimi, because on large pull requests the files containing the violations were often never opened, so they went back to a fixed pass, one call to the model for every changed file, and the share of violations found rose to between 91% and 100%. We did not repeat this measurement ourselves: the numbers are written in a comment in the source code of Kodus , which refers to their issue #1449 , and they concern a team’s own rules rather than bugs in general, but they show well enough what happens when the agent is left to decide where to look.

## How does OCR work?

OCR is a command-line tool written in Go, released under Apache-2.0, that runs in CI. This is how it reviews a pull request:

- It filters the changed files.

- It asks a model to group the related files.

- It plans the review.

- It runs one agent for each group, with a small set of tools: reading files, reading the diff, searching the code and writing a comment.

- Depending on the effort level, the agent runs one, two or three rounds, compressing its memory when the context grows too much.

- At the end a separate step removes the comments it can prove wrong.

- It writes a JSON report with the comments, the status of the review and the list of the files it covered, which is what you need to build a gate in CI.

It is not perfect, though: the feature we care about most, a partial review that declares itself partial and blocks the merge, is being worked on upstream but has been stuck for a couple of months, and while studying the code we found that the main loop ignores the reason why a model stopped generating. We wrote about both on the issue tracker, in #1489 and #1581 , and in the meantime we covered the gap with a small script of our own, which I describe below in “What We Added Around OCR”.

## How Did We Test It?

We tried the system on two of our open-source projects, LionWeb JVM and Starlasu Kotlin , and built three kinds of cases from their history:

- Historical bugs. We took commits that fixed a bug, ran git blame on the lines they changed and went back to the commit that had introduced the bug, to see whether the reviewer would have caught it, had it been there at that time.

- Pull requests we believed to be clean. We picked merged pull requests whose lines were still unchanged months later and whose files had received no fixes since. These measure the noise: everything the reviewer says on them should be, in theory, unnecessary (unless we have bugs we are unaware of, of course).

- Large pull requests , between 750 and 1,250 changed lines, to see whether the reviewer still does a good job when the change is too large to be read in one go.

We had hundreds of comments to read, so we gave that job to Fable 5.2. For each case it got the diff, the comments, what we already knew about the change and a checkout of the revision under review. We asked it to check each claim against the code and record its reasoning. A real bug meant there was something to fix. A useful comment made a valid, smaller point. Noise was the sort of observation you read, nod at and do nothing about. A wrong comment made a false or misleading claim. The percentages below use Fable’s judgments.

All the models were called through Mistral, which hosts its own models but also GLM 5.3 (flash and standard) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash . That means one key and one contract.

Why Mistral? Funny you asked, as I was going to explain that.

## Why Mistral?

For the development of code we use Claude Code and Codex, while for automations we use Mistral, which gives us a good ratio between quality and price, so it was the natural candidate also for the code reviews.

Then there is the question of the guarantees on the data. Simply, some of our clients require us to use solutions not just hosted in Europe but also controlled by a European company, because under the CLOUD Act the American authorities can ask American companies for the data they hold, wherever the servers are. We are also a European company and, when it is possible, we support European businesses. Being able to try Mistral’s own model alongside GLM and DeepSeek with the same API key made that preference easy to put to the test. Mistral Large earned its place on the results.

We also looked at whether another provider could lower the costs, and we did not find anything better. DeepSeek’s own API is cheap, but the data is processed and stored in China, and its peak hours, when the price doubles, are the European mornings. GLM on American hosts costs more than Mistral Large, and the other European hosts we found do not discount cached tokens, which for this workload roughly triples the bill.
